newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's LVMH gets tangled over DFS.
newsitem.headline: France's LVMH gets tangled over DFS.

text.p: Bernard Arnault, one of France's leading businessmen, who controls luxury goods company LVMH, Friday became entangled in a potential battle for control of U.S.-based duty free retailer DFS.

Shares LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton fell sharply in Paris, prompted by a Wall Street Journal report that investment house Kohlberg Kravis Roberts & Co. could mount a rival bid for DFS Group Ltd of San Francisco.

The leather goods, cognac and champagne group LVMH agreed in early October to buy a majority stake in DFS for $2.5 billion in order to extend its reach in the prosperous south east Asia and Pacific Rim regions.
The possibility of a bidding war against KKR, which won tobacco group R.J.R. Nabisco in the late 1980s, did not reassure investors and LVMH's stock fell in a rising Paris market.
LVMH closed 1.34 percent lower at 1,247 francs ($249) a share in a market that on average gained 1 percent.

A KKR spokesman in New York had no comment on the report that it might try to break LVMH's deal with two of the DFS group's four controlling shareholders, co-founder Charles Feeny and lawyer Alan M. Parker.
The transaction angered billionaire Robert Miller, who owns 38.75 percent of DFS, and financial advisr Anthony Pilaro, with a 2 percent stake.

Miller and Pilaro contend that Feeny and Parker went against a 1991 shareholders pact in agreeing to sell their stake to LVMH and they do not want to have a minority stake in a retailer which is controlled by one of its main suppliers.
The Miller camp has asked a mediator to arbitrate and have requested the commercial court in New York to suspend the LVMH deal until a solution is found.
DFS caters to the same group of affluent customers who buy LVMH's Louis Vuitton leather goods and designer luggage, Christian Dior perfumes, Hennessy cognacs and Moet & Chandon champagnes.
The Wall Street Journal said that KKR had told all four controlling DFS shareholders that it was willing to make a bid, without detailing possible financial terms.
